title: Composite Pattern
tagline: Model part-whole hierarchies so clients can treat individual objects and collections of objects through a single uniform interface.

sections.content:
**The Problem:** You have a tree structure — files and folders, UI widgets and panels, menu items and sub-menus. A `Folder` contains files AND other folders. You want to call `getSize()` on a `Folder` and have it recursively sum the sizes of everything inside, without the caller needing to know whether it is talking to a file or a folder. But without a pattern, the caller writes `if (item instanceof Folder) { ... } else { ... }` everywhere — fragile, repetitive, and closed to new node types.

**The Composite pattern** solves this by making both *leaf* nodes (File, Button) and *composite* nodes (Folder, Panel) implement the same interface (`FileSystemItem`, `Widget`). The composite's implementation of `getSize()` delegates recursively to its children — the caller calls `root.getSize()` and the recursion handles the rest, regardless of how deeply nested the tree is.

**Real-world trees that use this pattern:** file systems, DOM (every element can contain other elements), React component trees, UI toolkits, menu hierarchies, and expression trees in compilers.

sections.title: An Organisation Chart
sections.content:
An **Employee** has a salary. A **Department** also has a salary — but it's the sum of its employees' salaries (some of whom may themselves be department heads overseeing sub-departments). You want to call `getSalary()` on any node: individual or department, and get the correct total.

This is the Composite pattern: **treat the individual (leaf) and the group (composite) uniformly through the same operation**. The tree can be arbitrarily deep; the caller never changes.

**Participants:**

- **Component Interface** — declares the common operations for both leaves and composites. In our file system: `getName()`, `getSize()`, `print(indent)`. The client programs to this interface exclusively.
- **Leaf** — a primitive element with no children. Implements the Component Interface with concrete behaviour (a `File` knows its own size). Leaf nodes do the actual work in the tree.
- **Composite** — a container element. Stores a list of children (each a Component — leaf or composite). Implements Component methods by iterating children and aggregating: `getSize()` returns the sum of `child.getSize()` for all children. Also provides `add()` and `remove()` for managing children.
- **Client** — calls operations on the root Component. It never uses `instanceof` to distinguish leaf from composite — the recursion is entirely encapsulated.

**Transparency vs. Safety:** Some implementations put `add()`/`remove()` on the Component Interface (full transparency — client can call add on any node). Others put them only on Composite (safer — prevents callers from trying to add children to a leaf). The trade-off is compile-time safety vs. uniform treatment.

**Recursive delegation:** The composite's `getSize()` is beautifully simple: `return this._children.reduce((sum, child) => sum + child.getSize(), 0)`. The recursion terminates naturally at leaves (which return a scalar).

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: The File `getSize()` returns a scalar. The Folder `getSize()` returns the sum of its children — which may themselves be Folders. The recursion terminates naturally. The UI example shows the same pattern applied to render-time estimation of a component tree.

sections.label: Concept
sections.explanation: The skeleton makes it clear how the recursion unwinds: each composite calls `operation()` on each child, and the result bubbles up. The tree can be arbitrarily deep with no changes to clientCode.

sections.content:
**When to use:** Whenever your domain has a natural part-whole (tree) hierarchy: file systems, UI widget trees, organisational hierarchies, menus, expression trees, bill-of-materials. The pattern pays off as soon as a client would otherwise need to write `if (x instanceof Leaf)` branches.

**When NOT to use:** When your structure is shallow or fixed (no real hierarchy) — the pattern adds complexity. Also avoid if leaf and composite operations are radically different; forcing a common interface produces awkward no-op implementations.

**In the wild:** The HTML DOM (every `Element` can contain other `Element`s — `innerHTML`, `append()`, `querySelectorAll()` work uniformly). React component trees. Java's `javax.swing` component model. Apache POI document model. Expression trees in query builders.

items: The **Composite** pattern lets clients treat individual objects (leaves) and groups (composites) identically through a shared interface — eliminating `instanceof` checks.
**Recursive delegation** is the engine: a composite's operation calls the same operation on each child, which terminates at leaves that return scalar values.
The tree can be **arbitrarily deep** — the client code stays the same whether there are 2 levels or 20.
The **Folder-File** and **DOM Element** hierarchies are the canonical real-world examples; the pattern appears wherever you have part-whole relationships.

The trade-off between **transparency** (add/remove on the Component interface) and **safety** (add/remove only on Composite) depends on whether you want maximum uniformity or compile-time type correctness.

quiz.question: What is the core problem the Composite pattern solves?
options: Converting incompatible interfaces
Treating individual objects and groups of objects uniformly through a single interface
Deferring expensive object creation
Adding behaviour to objects at runtime
quiz.explanation: The Composite pattern's purpose is uniform treatment of leaf nodes and composite nodes — the client calls the same operation on either without needing instanceof checks.

quiz.question: In a Folder-File file system, which participant is the Leaf?
options: Folder — because it contains children
File — because it has no children and returns a scalar size
FileSystemItem — because it defines the interface
The client code that calls getSize()
quiz.explanation: A Leaf is a node with no children that implements the Component Interface directly with concrete behaviour. A File has no children — it returns its own fixed size.

quiz.question: How does `Folder.getSize()` compute the total size of all nested files?
options: It uses a flat list of all files stored at construction time
It recurses: calls getSize() on each child; composites recurse further; leaves return scalars
It caches the result at add() time
It reads the filesystem directly
quiz.explanation: The composite delegates: `children.reduce((sum, c) => sum + c.getSize(), 0)`. Each child that is a Folder recursively does the same. Files return their own fixed size — the recursion terminates naturally.

quiz.question: What is the 'transparency vs. safety' trade-off in the Composite pattern?
options: Whether to use TypeScript or JavaScript
Whether add()/remove() live on the Component interface (transparent but allows calling add on a leaf) or only on Composite (safe but requires casting)
Whether to store children in an Array or a Map
Whether to make getSize() synchronous or asynchronous
quiz.explanation: If add()/remove() are on the Component interface, the client can call them on any node (fully uniform) but a Leaf has to handle or reject those calls. If they're only on Composite, it's type-safe but the client must distinguish composites when building the tree.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT a natural fit for the Composite pattern?
options: An HTML DOM where elements can contain other elements
A flat key-value configuration store with no hierarchy
A bill-of-materials where assemblies contain sub-assemblies and parts
An organisation chart where departments contain employees and sub-departments
quiz.explanation: A flat key-value store has no tree structure or part-whole hierarchy — there is nothing to compose. The other three examples are classic tree hierarchies.

quiz.question: After calling `root.getSize()` on a deeply nested tree, how many `instanceof` checks does the client need?
options: One per level of nesting
One for leaf, one for composite
Zero — the pattern encapsulates all type distinctions inside the tree nodes
One for the root node only
quiz.explanation: The entire point of the Composite pattern is to eliminate instanceof checks. The client calls the same method on the root; each node knows how to handle it — leaf or composite — internally.

quiz.question: The HTML DOM's `element.querySelectorAll('.btn')` works on any element, whether it contains 0 or 1000 children. Which design pattern does this reflect?
options: Singleton
Observer
Composite — every element is both a potential leaf and a potential container with the same interface
Strategy
quiz.explanation: Every DOM Element implements the same interface (querySelector, appendChild, children) regardless of whether it has children — the hallmark of the Composite pattern.

quiz.question: In the skeleton `Composite.operation()`, what does calling `c.operation()` on each child achieve?
options: It initialises each child node
It triggers the recursive descent — composites recurse, leaves return scalars — and results are aggregated
It prevents infinite loops
It validates the type of each child
quiz.explanation: This is the recursive delegation. Each child decides how to handle `operation()` — composites iterate their own children; leaves return a value. The tree unwinds from leaves back to root, aggregating at each composite.

quiz.question: Why is the Composite pattern NOT appropriate when leaf and composite operations are radically different?
options: The pattern requires identical implementations in leaf and composite
Forcing a shared interface produces awkward no-op implementations on leaf nodes for composite-only methods
JavaScript does not support tree structures
Recursion is too slow for radically different operations
quiz.explanation: If composite has methods that make no sense on leaves (e.g., add(), countChildren()), you end up with throw-not-implemented or empty bodies on Leaf — a sign the abstraction is forced. The pattern fits best when both types genuinely share the interface.

quiz.question: Given: root (Folder) → docs (Folder) → guide.pdf (150 KB) + notes.txt (5 KB), and root → README.md (2 KB). What does `root.getSize()` return?
options: 150 KB
155 KB
157 KB
2 KB
quiz.explanation: docs.getSize() = 150 + 5 = 155 KB. root.getSize() = docs.getSize() + README.md = 155 + 2 = 157 KB.
